component.name: Harmony
component.summary: Browse, search, and sync music across YouTube Music and Qobuz

description.p: Harmony is a desktop app for managing music playlists across YouTube Music and Qobuz. Search both services from one place, browse and edit playlists, and mirror or two-way sync a playlist from one service to the other with fuzzy track matching that surfaces ambiguous matches for review rather than guessing at them.
Features:

ul.li: Unified search across both services
Create, edit, and delete playlists on either service
Cross-service sync with a reviewable plan before anything is written
A remembered match cache and before-sync snapshots
Import and export playlists as M3U, CSV, or JSON
Discovery blending Last.fm, ListenBrainz, and native recommendations

description.p: Playback polish. A new Now Playing view shows the whole playing playlist or album beside large cover art. The Now Playing bar gains a stop button, and double-clicking a track plays it here. Skipping a track no longer occasionally jumps two. Casting to a Chromecast now shows a moving progress bar and a working volume slider.

Browse the music, not just search it. Every artist, album, and track now has its own page — click a name or right-click a row to open it. Artist pages carry a short bio, a chronological discography, and for a band a Wikipedia-style member-timeline chart with album markers. Track pages show who performed on the recording (where MusicBrainz has it).

Search got smarter: searching an artist leads with their albums in release order; searching a person (say a band's former singer) shows the albums they actually performed on — the band's records only during their time in it — not the ones before they joined or after they left.

Hardened credential sharing between instances: a copied YouTube login can no longer leave a peer labelled "signed in" against a dead token. The auth type is now always validated against the real token on both send and receive, and a superseded auth file is cleaned up.

The Discover page has been rebuilt to match the rest of the app — proper preference groups, combo rows, and status pages in a tidy centered column, replacing the old mismatched layout. Recommendations and the AI playlist builder now read consistently, with clearer states and copy.

One active stream per instance, done right. Choosing a different device in the Now Playing bar now moves the whole playing queue to it — stopping the old device — instead of leaving audio behind or starting a second stream. The Devices page also reflects whatever is playing the moment you open it, without having to touch the controls.
Casting to a Chromecast or Google TV now sends the full track details — title, artist, album, and cover art — so the device's on-screen player shows what's playing instead of just streaming audio.

Discovered devices now populate the desktop Devices list and the “play to” picker automatically — the same way the web client works — instead of hiding behind a click-to-add popup. The Devices page also scans on open, and a discovered device can be pinned to keep it.
The Flatpak now bundles the Chromecast library, so the desktop app can discover and cast to Chromecast and Google TV devices — previously that worked only on the server package.
Fixes the system tray: the status icon and its right-click Quit menu now register correctly instead of failing silently and flooding the log.

A broad fit-and-finish pass across all three clients. The desktop app gains real empty and loading states, a reworked Route Audio screen, account sign-out, and human error messages in place of raw exceptions. The web app moves to a proper icon set and design system with a cast-aware Now Playing bar and full keyboard access. The Android app gets a complete Material 3 theme, corrected insets and artwork, a smoother seek, confirmations, and consistent copy throughout.

Cast to more places. Chromecast and Google TV are now output targets alongside WiiM/UPnP, auto-discovered on the network. Devices on another instance's LAN show up too — tagged “via …” — and play through the instance that can reach them, so a remote server can cast to a speaker at home. The phone now announces itself on the mesh, so the desktop and server see it as an instance.

Instances now reach each other on the most direct address — a shared-subnet LAN hop is preferred over a Tailscale/VPN overlay, so same-network audio routing takes the fast path. The personal-key check is now constant-time.

The web Devices tab now auto-discovers WiiM/UPnP renderers on the instance's network — no manual configuration. Instances reached over a VPN or routed subnet (where mDNS can't reach) can be remembered by address, so they stay in the account-sync and audio-routing lists. And the installable web app now updates itself on reload — no more clearing the service worker after each release.

The web client's Devices tab works now — pick where playback goes (this browser or a WiiM/UPnP device). The Android app gets a proper theme: the Harmony palette with dark mode, Material You dynamic color on Android 12+, and a bolder Now Playing control.

Packaging fix: upgrading the Debian package now actually updates the running server. The install script was missing pip's --upgrade, so an existing virtualenv kept the previous version even though the new one was installed.
Headless-server credential fixes:

ul.li: Credentials now persist on a server. With no unlocked login keyring, a half-detected Secret Service made copied credentials look saved but never authenticate; the server now always uses the 0600 file store, so adopted credentials work and survive a restart.
That file store is now encrypted at rest with a key derived from the personal key — the same key that gates and encrypts credential copies — so on-disk secrets aren't plaintext.

description.p: Accounts page gains a "Sync accounts from another instance" button — pick a discovered instance (or type its host:port) and copy its credentials over, encrypted with the personal key, instead of using the API by hand. Saving the personal key now also keeps this browser authenticated, and the web app's cache is bumped so it refreshes.

Credential copies now cross the network encrypted — the copied secrets are sealed with a key derived from the personal key (PBKDF2 → Fernet), so they stay confidential on the wire even over plain HTTP. Only a holder of the matching key can decrypt them.
Federation: full instances copy credentials from a peer.

ul.li: A full instance (a second desktop, a headless server) with a matching personal key but no accounts of its own now pulls the streaming credentials from a peer — automatically on first boot, or on demand — so a fresh headless server becomes a working credential holder without the browser/OAuth onboarding dance. Light clients (phone, web) still just use the hub's credentials over the API, never copying them. The export is served only to a key-matching caller.

description.p: The Android client is now a full light client — everything the web UI does except signing in (accounts stay on the hub):

ul.li: Library: browse playlists, open and play them, create / rename / delete, and add or remove tracks.
Sync: pick a source and target playlist, preview the plan, apply.
Output picker: play a track to a WiiM/UPnP device the hub knows, not just the phone.

description.p: Alpha fix — "play the hub's audio on my phone" now works reliably:

ul.li: Instead of the hub pushing UDP to the phone (which a phone rarely receives — Wi-Fi isolation, cellular, VPN NAT all block inbound UDP), the hub now serves its live output as an MP3 stream the phone pulls over HTTP and plays with buffering. Works on Wi-Fi, VPN, or cellular.

description.p: Alpha follow-up — federation fixes, a polished phone client, and the phone audio bridge:

ul.li: The Android client shows album art, has a cleaner Now Playing and search, and can bridge audio: play a hub track on a UPnP/DLNA device on the phone's own network by relaying the stream through the phone — so it works even when the hub is reached over a VPN.

Fixes: "Play on this phone" now actually works (the RTP sender was mis-configured); instances advertise all their addresses (LAN + VPN) so roaming clients find a reachable one; expired stream URLs are re-resolved instead of failing a late seek; inter-instance routing negotiates a matching transport.

description.p: Alpha bundle — first release carrying every client + package together (desktop & server Flatpak, Debian server package, Android APK):

ul.li: Inter-instance audio routing: send or receive full system audio between instances over the mesh, with a Music-default / Gaming latency preset. Play another machine's audio here, or send this machine's to it.
The web client is now a mobile-friendly, installable PWA — a phone bottom-nav, touch controls, and offline app shell.
A headless-server Debian package that runs Harmony as a systemd service.
Fix: one unavailable track (no videoId) no longer fails a whole YouTube Music playlist.

description.p: The mesh milestone. Harmony instances now find each other and share a single account, and there is a mobile client:

ul.li: Every instance serves an HTTP API (and a lightweight web UI), always on when the app runs — the engine other clients talk to.
LAN discovery over mDNS: instances see one another automatically, and a light client (phone, another desktop) can join without its own logins.
Personal key: set one key across your instances and only matching keys may share credentials — the gate for account sharing on every version.
Zero-setup YouTube: one click detects the browser you are already signed in with (native or Flatpak) and connects — no OAuth dance.
Minimize to the system tray; a right-click there actually quits. The API server keeps running in the background.
A new Android client: discover an instance on your network, connect with your key, search, and play — streaming real hi-res audio from the hub.
Fixes: YouTube playlists load reliably again.

description.p: Playback and UI polish:

ul.li: The Now Playing seek bar now works reliably, with smooth second-by-second progress and a clear message when a track can't be seeked.
Right-click pickers (Play on Device / Add to Playlist) open under the pointer and stay on-screen, including for songs inside a playlist.
Local playback ("This computer") requests the highest-quality stream a track allows — Qobuz hi-res FLAC, YouTube's best audio — and shows the negotiated output format.
Now-playing indicators light up the playlist a track is playing from; a playlist's track view refreshes when tracks are added to it.

description.p: Milestone release. Harmony is now a full music hub, not just a playlist syncer:

ul.li: A persistent Now Playing bar with transport, seek, volume, shuffle/repeat, a device selector, and on-screen playing indicators.
Local playback ("This computer") — decode and play tracks on this machine through PipeWire, alongside casting to devices.
Route Audio — receive a low-latency network stream (ROC, with forward error correction) from another machine and play it locally.
Qobuz streaming reliability fixes, including recovering the app secret used to sign streaming requests.
Stability: a crash fix in album-art loading, log files for easier diagnosis, and clean shutdown of routed streams.

description.p: Fixes a crash (segfault) that could happen while album art loaded in the Now Playing bar: the artwork texture was being created on a worker thread, which isn't safe for GTK. Also writes logs to a rotating file (cache/harmony/harmony.log) so problems are easier to diagnose.

A Route Audio receiver no longer keeps running after you close the app: it's stopped on window close, and any survivor is terminated when the app exits — so a routed stream can't be left playing with no way to stop it.

"This computer" (local playback) now appears in every play-to-device picker — the Search toolbar, Discover, and the Similar dialog — not just the right-click menu. Also clearer Qobuz sign-in guidance in the setup script, which now leads with the reliable token option.

Adds an in-app local player: pick "This computer" as a playback target to decode and play a track (e.g. a Qobuz FLAC) on this machine through PipeWire, controlled from the Now Playing bar like any device. Uses GStreamer, already in the runtime.
The currently-playing track now shows a play indicator next to it in search results and playlist views, updating live as playback moves through a queue.

Adds a persistent Now Playing bar along the bottom of the window: album art, title/artist, play-pause, previous/next, a draggable seek bar, a volume slider (for devices that support it), shuffle and repeat, and a device selector. Playback state is now centralized app-wide, so the bar reflects and controls whatever is playing to a device.

Route Audio (ROC) now rides through brief Wi-Fi stalls instead of tearing down the session. roc's watchdog dropped the session after only 133ms of blank audio, so a momentary network hiccup caused a pop; widening the blank tolerance to 2s (and choppy to 4s) lets playback resume seamlessly, keeping latency low without the occasional ticks.

Fixes the root cause of Route Audio (ROC) dropouts: the receiver was restarting its session dozens of times a second because the latency tolerance was too tight, so normal latency fluctuation kept crossing the bound. Widening it yields a single stable session (diagnosed from a verbose loopback: ~79 restarts in 15s before, 1 after).

Fixes frequent audio dropouts on Route Audio (ROC): roc-recv's log no longer goes to an undrained pipe that could stall playback, the resampler is now high-quality, jitter tolerance is wider, and the default target latency has more headroom for Wi-Fi. Diagnostics are written to a log file. Raise the target latency if audio still breaks up.

Route Audio now uses ROC when available (bundled in the Flatpak): forward error correction and an adaptive latency tuner keep network audio glitch-free at far lower latency than plain RTP over Wi-Fi. Falls back to RTP where roc-recv isn't present.
New Route Audio page: receive a low-latency RTP audio stream from another machine on your LAN (e.g. a Steam Deck) and play it out a chosen local output device. Works in the Flatpak.
Playlists can now export to and import from a plain, human-readable text list (one "Artist - Title" per line, with the track's universal ISRC id appended where known so it re-resolves exactly).
Album/playlist queue playback now advances to the next track based on playback position reaching the track's duration, which is reliable across devices, instead of a device-specific stop signal.

Right-click context menus now cover collections: play a whole album, artist, or playlist to a device, or add all of its tracks to a playlist, in one action. Tracks in a playlist get the same full menu as search.

Discover page overhaul: recommendation results are now actionable (play to a device or add to a playlist right from the list), with live progress while suggestions load, a Regenerate button, clearer empty states, and friendlier source labels.

Play-to-device now uses UPnP so the renderer's own screen can show the track (title, artist, album art) and report a duration, and the Devices page shows a live progress bar. Falls back automatically to direct control if a device has no UPnP support.
Adds right-click context menus across tracks, artists, albums, and playlists, and a "Show Similar" music action that opens a recommendations view you can play or turn into a playlist.
Adds selectable color themes (Appearance in Preferences), fixes YouTube tracks cutting off partway through when playing to a device, and makes the Devices page show the playing track reliably.
Unified search and cross-service playlist sync across YouTube Music and Qobuz, discovery, WiiM/LinkPlay device control, and play-to-device (a passive LAN relay that streams a track to a speaker).
Initial packaged release.
